Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

whole adjective and noun

all of, entire

also entire, all of, the whole, as a whole, all day long

classical

Plin. Ep. 7.3.2: līber tōtus diēs
Plaut. Persa 114–115: id tōtum prōcēdit diem
Quint. 6.3.9: tōtum corpus vī suā concutit
Traupman 407

tōtus, tōta, tōtum

adjective; genitive tōtīus, dative tōtī, declension

whole, entire, all of

With a word of time the accusative alone means “all … long” (tōtum diem); with other nouns Latin uses per: per tōtum iter, the whole way.

Other words

  • ūniversus, ūniversa, ūniversum — whole, all together; as a whole

    declension · also used · classical · Tac. Agr. 12.2: singulī pugnant, ūniversī vincuntur; Tac. Germ. 5.1: in ūniversum, “on the whole”

  • omnis, omne — all, every; the whole of (a thing taken as one)

    declension · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.1.1: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs

  • cūnctus, cūncta, cūnctum — all together, the whole

    declension · also used · classical · Traupman 407

    Mostly in the plural: cūnctī, all of them together.

Examples

  • Māne quod tū occēperis negōtium agere, id tōtum prōcēdit diem.

    Whatever business you start in the morning goes well the whole day.Plaut. Persa 114–115

  • quoūsque calceī nusquam, toga fēriāta, līber tōtus diēs?

    how long will it be no shoes, the toga on holiday, the whole day free?Plin. Ep. 7.3.2

  • jānua nē versō strīdōrēs cardine reddat, nūlla domō tōtā est

    so that no door may creak on its turning hinge, there is not one in the whole houseOv. Met. 11.608–609

See also whole, half, part, all, the top of.
